description: Resource-based view cluster The RBV cluster is the largest in terms of size and volume (number of articles 5 70) and the publications on this topic appeared between 1997 and 2022. It predominantly comprises the following keywords: RBV; practice-based view; conceptual theory building; marketing capability; SMEs; and integrative framework. Table A1 in Appendix provides more information about this cluster’s most significant authors, who were selected based on their citation scores. Five subtopics were identified in this cluster. 4.1.1 Competitive advantage. This area is covered by 10 studies. Some studies focus on the impacts of resources, competencies and DCs on different types of eco-innovation (e.g. Kiefer et al., 2019). Other researchers studied human resource practices’ contribution to firms’ SCAs (e.g. Delery and Roumpi, 2017). A third set of authors examined sustainable supply chain management as a way to generate valuable interorganizational resources and sustained interfirm competitive advantages (e.g. Gold et al., 2010). 4.1.2 Information technology (IT). Twelve studies were published on this subtopic. Some researchers studied IT capabilities’ effect on firm resources and the fit between different types of IT competencies and firm resources (e.g. Stoel and Muhanna, 2009). Others focused on green human resource management practices as internal resources that can stimulate employees’ pro-environmental IT behavior (e.g. Ojo et al., 2020). 4.1.3 Complementarity. This subtopic includes 36 documents, which are focused on the integration of institutional theory and the RBV (e.g. Ipek and Tanyeri, 2021) and on how the supply chain practice view can complement the practice-based view, RBV and relational view (e.g. Carter et al., 2017). Other studies are based on the combination of contemporary entrepreneurship and RBV theories (e.g. Foss et al., 2008). 4.1.4 SMEs. This subtopic includes seven research articles, of which some focus on the association between SMEs’ e-commerce investment and firm performance from an RBV perspective (e.g. Yang et al., 2015). Another set of authors examined the relationships between social networks, supply chain resilience and customer-oriented performance in SMEs (e.g. Asamoah et al., 2020). 4.1.5 Value, rare, inimitable and organization (VRIO). Five studies were published on this subtopic to investigate what happens when the value, rare, inimitable and organization (VRIO) approach informs strategic initiatives and how users select which resources to evaluate (e.g. Knott, 2015), to evaluate companies’ internal activities, including using fuzzy utility functions to identify available resources’ competitive advantage (e.g. Lin et al., 2012). Other publications comprise the analysis of the entrepreneurship research with the VRIO model used as a strategic tool (e.g. Lopes et al., 2021). A final set analyzes the O in VRIO to show how resources’ benefits depend on the way they are deployed in organizations’ workflow (e.g. Kim and Makadok, 2021). Being the largest cluster, the RBV naturally presents the highest number of links between topics. Specifically, the subtopic of competitive advantage demonstrates interrelationships with SMEs’ firm performance, location effects and customer orientation. Competitive advantage is also connected with the VRIO and information technology subtopics. Finally, complementarity topic and VRIO as a strategic tool mutually influence each other, encompassing aspects such as resource evaluation and firm performance.

Customer orientation and Alliance Portfolio Cluster This cluster is the smallest in terms of size and volume (number 5 16) and the main keywords found within this cluster are alliance portfolio, inter-cluster alliance and alliance portfolio configuration. Table A2 in Appendix offers more details on the most important authors based on their citation scores. The publication timeline runs between 2011 and 2022. 4.2.1 Customer relationship management (CRM). This subtopic includes five studies. Some of them concentrate on service-related resources’ effects on trade fair exhibitor personnel’s attitudes and visitors’ responses (Jha et al., 2019). Other authors are interested in customer relationship management (CRM) and technology capabilities, developing measurement scales assessing clients’ perception of CRM initiatives (Dubey and Sangle, 2019). 4.2.2 Alliance portfolio. Eleven articles cover this subtopic. Some are case studies focused on, for example, alliance portfolios’ exploration versus exploitation orientation and how this improves firm performance depending on internal organizational characteristics, strategic orientations and industry environments (e.g. Yamakawa et al., 2011). Other studies examine the configuration of inter-cluster alliance portfolios according to the available resources and capabilities, alliance strategy, and environmental conditions, from the perspective of the RBV, DCs and social network theories (e.g. Colovic, 2019). Being the smallest cluster, it is naturally the one with the lowest number of links and both CRM and alliance portfolio topics are oriented toward the external environment.

Resource-based theory cluster This cluster’s publication timeline is between 2001 and 2022 and comprises four subtopics, forming the fourth biggest group in terms of size and volume (number 5 28). The prevalent keywords within this cluster include resource-based theory, stakeholder theory, incomplete contract theory, resource management and open innovation. Table A3 in Appendix presents this cluster’s most significant authors, who were chosen based on their citation scores. 4.3.1 Marketing capability. Four studies are dedicated to this subtopic, of which two are highlighted here. The first assessed social media resources and DCs that enhance firms’ social media performance using measurement scales (Marchand et al., 2021). The second example focuses on linking resource capabilities and performance by incorporating social and business networks, international experience and marketing capabilities (Jeong et al., 2019). 4.3.2 Stakeholder theory. This subtopic includes five studies. The first set suggests that managers need to recognize that all stakeholders have a legitimate claim on the profits generated by their firm’s resources (Barney, 2018). The remaining studies examine the association between corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities and top management’s position in social hierarchies (i.e. network centrality) (e.g. Chen et al., 2021). 4.3.3 Open innovation. The nine publications on this subtopic argue that crowdsourcing can become a valuable asset if firms can extract value from it (e.g. Cappa et al., 2019) and explore manufacturing SMEs’ adoption and use of information systems (ISs) and information technology (IT) as key drivers of long-term successful IS and/or IT deployment based on these firms’ organizational competencies (e.g. Caldeira and Ward, 2001). 4.3.4 Resource management. This subtopic includes ten studies that reveal managerial actions’ important role in effectively structuring, bundling and leveraging firm resources. The research includes comparisons of resource management and asset orchestration frameworks (e.g. Sirmon et al., 2011), the analysis of relationships between value-chain dynamics, market sensing capability and performance on franchise outlets’ success (e.g. Zimuto and Maritz, 2019), and the identification of companies’ dormant resources (e.g. Felin et al., 2021). According to the research studies within this cluster, stakeholder theory (pertaining to stakeholder perspectives and claims on profits) is linked to open innovation (encompassing product, process, marketing and service innovation). The latter is also connected to resource management and marketing capability (including CRM, communication and their relationship with firm performance) topics.

Firm performance cluster This cluster comes fifth in terms of size and volume (number 5 26). The publications on this topic appeared in journals between 1994 and 2022 and include some of the following keywords: firm performance, SCA, organizational innovativeness, innovation and absorptive capacity. Three subtopics were identified in the cluster. Table A4 in Appendix provides additional information on the most important authors in firm performance research. 4.4.1 Sustainable performance. This subtopic includes 12 studies. Among other subjects, the articles focused on the negative relationship between government subsidies and firm performance from a resource-based perspective (e.g. Song et al., 2021). Other publications cover resource-based theory’s role in enhancing business performance and SCAs through strategic internal resources and innovative activities (e.g. Çagl   ıyan et al., 2022). Finally, a group of authors explored the benefits of implementing green strategies by paying attention to too-much-of-a-good-thing and too-little-of-a-good-thing effects (e.g. Lin et al., 2021a). 4.4.2 Absorptive capacity. Ten articles were published on this subtopic. Some studies sought to establish whether the link between green business strategy and firm performance is positively moderated by internal absorptive capacity and the public’s environmental concerns (e.g. Lin et al., 2021b). Other studies reveal that high-agile firms with greater absorptive capacity are more innovative and better performers than low-agile firms (e.g. Martinez-Sanchez et al., 2019). Six studies focused on how organizations’ structural factors (i.e. decentralization, formalization and specialization) affect firms’ capacity for logistics service innovation and firm performance (e.g. Daugherty et al., 2011). 4.4.3 Institutional theory. Four studies were published on this subtopic, focusing on the complex connections between institutionalized norms, core competencies and systematic differences in firms’ willingness to imitate (e.g. Jonsson and Regner, 2009). Other authors expanded the RBV’s boundaries by incorporating institutional factors related to societal and political issues (e.g. Auh and Menguc, 2009). The institutional theory topic encompasses institutionalized norms, core competencies and societal and political issues. In turn, absorptive capacity topic relates to the ability to acquire, assimilate and use external knowledge. Thus, both institutional theory and absorptive capacity influence and shape firms’ sustainable performance.

Entrepreneurial orientation cluster This cluster has the second biggest size and volume (number 5 44). Studies on this subtopic were published between 2003 and 2022. The main keywords within this cluster encompass talent management, value creation, intellectual capital and stakeholder management. Four subtopics were detected in this cluster.Table A5 in Appendix presents more details on the most prominent researchers within the field of EO, who were selected based on their citation scores. 4.5.1 Intellectual capital. The seven studies related to this subtopic cover two areas, among others. The first is the potential for reducing organizations’ decision uncertainty by tapping into their intellectual capital and operating environment (e.g. Herremans et al., 2011). The second area is intellectual capital’s mediating role in the relationship between corporate governance mechanisms and bank performance (e.g. Aslam and Haron, 2021). 4.5.2 Firm value. This subtopic is explored by nine articles. The majority are directly related to the concepts of value creation, value capture, value leverage and value protection. Some authors analyzed the value of individual talent and talent management architecture (e.g. Sparrow and Makram, 2015). Other researchers compared high versus low levels of environmental dynamism, competition intensity and firm capability to clarify the relationship between corporate social investment and firm value (e.g. Sun and Ding, 2021). 4.5.3 Firm resources. Twenty eight studies covered this subtopic. For example, one group of authors linked strategies for expanding firms’ products and geographic markets to actions taken to manage resources (e.g.Holcomb et al., 2009). Another set of researchers focused on innovations in supply chain communication systems that can be understood as an internal resource that enhances channel capabilities, which in turn affects firms’ market performance (Kim et al., 2006). 4.5.4 Strategic management. There are twenty research studies on this subtopic. For example, a dynamic capability approach is presented by integrating the internal (resourcebased theory) and external (resource-dependency theory) perspectives. The results show that the ambidexterity found in innovation and social networks mediate the relationship between EO and firm performance in SMEs (Nofiani et al., 2021). Another study used the VRIO framework to provide the theoretical foundations of CSR implementation, in the form of corporate giving to charities, to develop a dynamic capability and, thus, lead to the better management of stakeholders (Cantrell et al., 2015). The connections within the EO cluster underscore its pervasive influence across the following key subtopics: (1) strategic management, impacting ambidexterity in innovation and social networks, and establishing relationships between capabilities, advantages and firms’ performance; (2) intellectual capital, involving social and business networks, and playing a mediating role in governance and performance; (3) firm resources, directly affecting firms’ capabilities and strategic orientation—both entrepreneurial and market-focused; and (4) firm value, establishing connections with CSR and directly linking to value creation, capture, leverage and protection.

Dynamic capabilities cluster This cluster appears in the center of the map, coming third in terms of size and volume (number 5 42) and presents some of the following keywords: competitive strategy, dynamic capabilities, competences and management strategy. The publications appeared between 1997 and 2022. Four subtopics were identified in this cluster. Table A6 in Appendix presents further information on the most important researchers within the DCs field, who were chosen based on their citation scores. 4.6.1 Competitive strategy. Thirteen studies were published on this subject. Some authors assert that capabilities can be categorized according to the corresponding resources, activities and internal-external focus, which allows firms to tailor their sustainability strategies to fit their needs and thus engage in competitive leveraging (e.g. McDougall et al., 2021). In addition, companies develop varied capabilities through cooperation that sustain competitive advantages contributing to superior performance (Wilke et al., 2019). 4.6.2 Competencies. This subtopic includes five studies. Some researchers focused on determining whether DCs (i.e. internal market orientation and information and communications technology competence) affect the development of different products, processes, marketing strategies and organizational social innovations (e.g. Sanzo-Perez et al., 2015). Other key factors are control over residual material flows, adjustments in human resources, management of environmental constraints, and networking and marketing tactics (e.g. Kabongo and Boiral, 2017). 4.6.3 Resources. This topic is covered by 15 studies presenting evidence that DCs are part of a system that includes resources and strategies, which together determine the competitive advantages each firm can gain over its rivals (e.g. Teece, 2018). A final set argues that resources and capabilities must evolve as new strategic challenges emerge (e.g. West and Taplin, 2016). 4.6.4 Human resource management. This subtopic includes nine studies asserting that a connection exists between employment, internal liquidity of labor, organizational routines and internal cooperation (e.g. Shereret al., 1998). Other authors argue that providing strategic human capital to other firms within alliances can be a way to leverage resources and that strategic knowledge facilitates transactions between companies with co-specialized human capital and tangible resources (e.g. Ferrary, 2015)
